title: How many early printed editions have been lost without trace?
short: Estimates of the share of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century editions that survive in no copy vary widely, and depend on statistical models that have rarely been tested against later discoveries.
matters: Quantitative histories of the early book trade, of literacy and of the spread of ideas count surviving editions as if they were a fixed fraction of what was printed. If loss was heavy and uneven, falling hardest on cheap, small-format, vernacular, ephemeral and heavily used books such as schoolbooks, almanacs, broadsides and devotional texts, then the apparent dominance of Latin learned printing and the relative output of regions and printers are artefacts of survival. The same estimates are used to calibrate long-run series of book production that feed into economic history.
stuck: Lost editions leave evidence only indirectly, in booksellers' catalogues, inventories, references, binding fragments and editions known from a single copy. Statistical estimates depend on assumptions about how copy counts are distributed, and the main models give different answers for different categories of book. Catalogues such as ISTC, GW and USTC are revised continuously, but no one has systematically used their revision history to test whether past estimates correctly predicted the rate and kind of new discoveries.
solved: A survival model fitted on a dated snapshot of a major catalogue (for example ISTC or USTC as of a past year) that correctly predicts the number and category distribution of editions added in later years, together with an estimate of total lost editions by format, language and genre with stated uncertainty.
approach: The estimates so far rest on a few decisions made differently each time: Buringh and van Zanden (2009) applied assumed loss rates, Green et al. (2011) and Green and McIntyre (2016) fitted copy-count distributions from ISTC, and Kestemont and Karsdorp (2020) and Kestemont et al. (2022) brought ecological unseen-species estimators from Efron and Thisted (1976) to manuscripts, with open code. Camps, Randon-Furling and Godreau (2025) have since set manuscript and incunable loss rates side by side.

Turning the catalogues into data means one record per edition with its surviving copy count, format, language, genre and sheet count. How copies are counted shapes the result, since fragments in bindings, Sammelbände and duplicate holdings in aggregated catalogues all inflate or deflate the singletons on which the estimators depend; Proot (2016) shows why sheet count and institutional ownership belong in the model.

With that table built from ISTC, GW, USTC and VD16, Chao1, Efron–Thisted and their successors can be fitted separately by format, language and genre, so that cheap vernacular print, which Pettegree (2016) and Eisermann (2016) argue is the most heavily lost, is not averaged away.

Catalogues have histories, so the estimators can be tested. Reconstructing earlier states of ISTC and GW from published versions and dated records, and checking what each snapshot predicted against the editions found since, would show which estimator is calibrated; that comparison is useful whatever the final total.

The documentary record of lost books is a second, independent check: registered titles in the Stationers' Register as used by Hill (2016), booksellers' lists, inventories and privileges, as gathered by Bruni and Pettegree (2016). Where statistical and documentary estimates diverge, the gap itself measures how far copy-count models miss editions that left no survivor at all, and the total will remain a range.

The catalogues are online, so no new digitization is needed, but dated record histories depend on cooperation from their maintainers at CERL, the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin and St Andrews, and book historians should review how fragments and ephemera are classified.

existing.title: Estimating the number of unseen species: How many words did Shakespeare know?
existing.note: Adapted ecological unseen-species estimation to texts, the methodological ancestor of later estimates of lost books.

existing.authors: Eltjo Buringh and Jan Luiten van Zanden
existing.title: Charting the 'Rise of the West': Manuscripts and Printed Books in Europe, A Long-Term Perspective from the Sixth through Eighteenth Centuries
existing.note: Estimated European manuscript and book production by century, applying assumed loss rates to surviving counts; widely used and criticized for its survival assumptions.

existing.authors: Jonathan Green, Frank McIntyre and Paul Needham
existing.title: The Shape of Incunable Survival and Statistical Estimation of Lost Editions
existing.venue: Papers of the Bibliographical Society of America 105 (2): 141–175
existing.note: Fitted distributions to ISTC copy counts and argued that lost incunable editions are far more numerous than earlier guesses, especially among small editions.

existing.authors: Flavia Bruni and Andrew Pettegree, eds.
existing.title: Lost Books: Reconstructing the Print World of Pre-Industrial Europe
existing.venue: Leiden: Brill (Library of the Written Word 46)
existing.note: Collected case studies of documented but lost editions across Europe, using inventories, catalogues and archival references.

existing.title: The Legion of the Lost: Recovering the Lost Books of Early Modern Europe
existing.venue: In Bruni and Pettegree, eds., Lost Books (Leiden: Brill), 1–27
existing.note: Argued from USTC data that a large share of sixteenth-century editions, especially cheap vernacular print, survive in one copy or none.

existing.title: The Gutenberg Galaxy's Dark Matter: Lost Incunabula, and Ways to Retrieve Them
existing.venue: In Bruni and Pettegree, eds., Lost Books (Leiden: Brill), 29–54
existing.note: Surveyed the documentary and fragmentary evidence for lost fifteenth-century editions, including broadsides and indulgences recovered from bindings.

existing.title: Lost Incunable Editions: Closing in on an Estimate
existing.venue: In Bruni and Pettegree, eds., Lost Books (Leiden: Brill), 55–72
existing.note: Refined the 2011 estimates of how many fifteenth-century editions survive in no copy.

existing.title: Lost Print in England: Entries in the Stationers' Company Register, 1557–1640
existing.venue: In Bruni and Pettegree, eds., Lost Books (Leiden: Brill), 144–159
existing.note: Used registered titles with no surviving copy to measure loss in English print, an independent check on statistical estimates.

existing.title: Survival Factors of Seventeenth-Century Hand-Press Books Published in the Southern Netherlands: The Importance of Sheet Counts, Sammelbände and the Role of Institutional Collections
existing.venue: In Bruni and Pettegree, eds., Lost Books (Leiden: Brill), 160–201
existing.note: Showed that survival depends strongly on edition size in sheets, binding with other works and institutional ownership, variables a survival model should include.

existing.title: Estimating the Loss of Medieval Literature with an Unseen Species Model from Ecodiversity
existing.venue: Proceedings of the Workshop on Computational Humanities Research (CHR 2020), CEUR Workshop Proceedings 2723
existing.note: Applied the Chao1 estimator to Middle Dutch chivalric epics and compared it with other estimators on simulated data, the pilot for the 2022 Science study.

existing.authors: Mike Kestemont, Folgert Karsdorp, Elisabeth de Bruijn, Matthew Driscoll, Katarzyna A. Kapitan, Pádraig Ó Macháin, Daniel Sawyer and Remco Sleiderink
existing.title: Forgotten books: The application of unseen species models to the survival of culture
existing.note: Applied unseen-species models to medieval narrative manuscripts in six vernaculars and estimated that most works survive but most manuscripts were lost, with marked differences between literatures; data and code released openly.

existing.authors: Jean-Baptiste Camps, Julien Randon-Furling and Ulysse Godreau
existing.title: On the transmission of texts: written cultures as complex systems
existing.note: Compiles loss-rate estimates for medieval manuscripts and incunabula and models textual transmission as a complex system.
